title: Public Health Consulting and Program Coordination
summary: Senior consulting role leading and coordinating multiple concurrent public health projects, advising clients on social justice programming, and supporting partnerships, facilitation, and implementation.
context: The Michigan Public Health Institute supports public health organizations, agencies, and communities through consulting, evaluation, and program services. Fayana served as a Senior Public Health Consultant from June 2021 to 2025, working across multiple client engagements at the same time.
need: Client organizations needed help translating public health and social justice priorities into organized, well-managed programs — from initial intake and scoping through implementation, facilitation, and partnership management.
goals: Define each client's needs clearly and convert them into actionable scopes of work.
Keep concurrent projects organized, on schedule, and visible to stakeholders.
Support clients in addressing racism, oppression, and health disparities through credible, well-facilitated programming.
Maintain strong, accountable partnerships across organizations.
stakeholders: Client organizations, organizational leaders, internal consulting teams, supervised staff, and community and organizational partners.
scope: Multiple concurrent public health consulting projects, including social justice programming, workshop design and facilitation, partnership support, and project planning and monitoring.
responsibilities: Coordinated six concurrent projects and workstreams, aligning timelines, deliverables, and stakeholder communication with organizational and client priorities.
Led weekly team meetings and individual check-ins for project teams of four to nine members, preparing agendas, directing action-item follow-up, reviewing milestones, and assigning responsibilities.
Conducted client intake meetings, developed and monitored scopes of work, and supported contracts, partnership agreements, and joint-venture agreements.
Designed and facilitated more than 50 workshops, including virtual sessions addressing racism, oppression, health disparities, and related public health issues.
Submitted quarterly progress summaries and final reports to funding agencies, collaborative partners, and clients, and co-monitored budgets with the Senior Financial Analyst.
Managed sensitive issues and escalations and advised organizational leaders.
Supervised and mentored two staff members and reviewed work produced by research scientists and research and evaluation associates.
Co-wrote five concept papers with collaborative partners for grant opportunities.
planning: Engagements began with client intake meetings to clarify needs, goals, and constraints. Fayana translated those discussions into scopes of work and project plans with defined timelines, milestones, responsibilities, and deliverables, and she maintained tracking tools to keep progress visible.
implementation: She coordinated internal and external stakeholders across concurrent workstreams, facilitated meetings and workshops, monitored deliverables against plans, managed sensitive issues and escalations as they arose, and adjusted plans based on new information.
methods: Used qualitative and quantitative information to support program decisions, including stakeholder feedback and project-tracking data.
deliverables: Toolkits, concept papers, and facilitation guides
Workshop series and facilitated virtual sessions
Quarterly progress summaries and final reports
Scopes of work and project plans
Advisory support to clients and organizational leaders
risks: Work involved sensitive public health topics, multiple concurrent commitments, and confidential client relationships, requiring careful issue management, escalation support, and disciplined documentation.
results: Coordinated six concurrent projects and workstreams through to delivery.
Designed and facilitated more than 50 workshops for public health professionals and clients.

Delivered toolkits, concept papers, a statewide strategic plan, workshop series, and facilitation guides for audiences including grant agencies, public health professionals, older adults living with disabilities or dementia and their caregivers, and government officials.
Co-wrote five concept papers with collaborative partners for grant opportunities.
Supervised and mentored two staff members.
resultsNote: Public outcome details are limited because the work involved confidential organizational information.
lessons: Concurrent consulting work reinforced the value of early scoping, visible tracking, and direct, timely communication when sensitive issues arise.
confidentialityNote: Client names, project names, contract information, and partner names are not published. Selected project details have been summarized to protect organizational confidentiality.

title: Community-Engaged Research on Aging, Caregiving, and Chronic Illness
summary: Doctoral research examining aging, caregiving, chronic illness, and health disparities among older Black women in Detroit, based on approximately 18 months of field research.
context: As a doctoral researcher in medical anthropology at Michigan State University, Fayana designed and conducted an extended community-based research project in Detroit between 2010 and 2017.
need: Health disparities affecting older Black women are shaped by social and structural conditions that are difficult to capture without sustained, community-engaged research. The project required careful research design, long-term field engagement, and respectful relationships with participants.
goals: Understand how aging, caregiving, and chronic illness are experienced by older Black women in Detroit.
Examine the social and structural determinants shaping those experiences.
Produce rigorous scholarly work grounded in community-engaged methods.
stakeholders: Research participants, community members in Detroit, university faculty and advisors, and funding organizations.
scope: Approximately 18 months of field research, including qualitative data collection, interviews, and analysis of qualitative and quantitative information.
responsibilities: Designed and conducted field-based research over approximately 18 months.
Conducted interviews and collected qualitative information.
Collected or analyzed quantitative information.
Examined social and structural determinants of health.
Produced scholarly work and developed expertise in research design, data collection, analysis, and research communication.
planning: The research required a defined design, participant engagement approach, and data collection plan developed through doctoral training and supported by competitive funding.
implementation: Fayana carried out sustained fieldwork in Detroit, building the relationships and trust needed for community-engaged research on sensitive topics including illness, caregiving, and aging.
methods: Ethnographic field research, qualitative interviews, and analysis of qualitative and quantitative information.
deliverables: Completed doctoral research and dissertation (2018 PhD conferral)
Scholarly work based on the research
risks: Research involving older adults and sensitive health topics required careful attention to participant privacy, respectful engagement, and accurate representation of findings.
results: The research was supported by multi-year funding from Michigan State University and the National Science Foundation, including an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship (2011–2014).
The work led to the completion of her Doctor of Philosophy in Medical Anthropology in 2018.
lessons: Sustained field research strengthened Fayana's conviction that reliable evidence and lived experience belong together in public health work — a perspective she carries into program design and evaluation.
confidentialityNote: Participant identities, the dissertation title, participant counts, award amounts, and detailed findings are not published here pending verification and approval. Research participants are never identified.

title: Research and Professional Development Program for Underrepresented Students
summary: Helped develop a research and professional development program for students from underrepresented backgrounds and supported a National Institutes of Health R01 grant application.
context: During her postdoctoral appointment at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, affiliated with the Center for Community Health Research, Fayana contributed to community-engaged research on chronic disease prevention and transnational health.
need: The center sought to expand research opportunities and professional development for students from underrepresented backgrounds, and to prepare a competitive National Institutes of Health (NIH) R01 grant application with sound staffing, budget, and compliance plans.
goals: Build a structured research and professional development program for underrepresented students.
Support the preparation of an NIH R01 grant application.
Coordinate research and professional development activities across faculty, staff, students, and community partners.
stakeholders: Faculty, staff, students, community partners, and the Center for Community Health Research.
scope: Program design and coordination, grant application support (staffing, budget, and compliance planning), and community-engaged research support.
responsibilities: Designed and implemented a professional development curriculum for students from underrepresented backgrounds, expanding access to research training and institutional support.
Supported NIH R01 proposal development by drafting, editing, and conducting compliance reviews of grant requirements and budget preparation.
Coordinated input across faculty and administrative stakeholders to ensure the timely, accurate, and compliant submission of a competitive funding proposal.
Collaborated with a Community Research Liaison and Project Manager to strengthen the Center for Community Health Research's Community Steering Board.
Supported community-engaged research on chronic disease prevention and transnational health, including targeted literature reviews.
planning: Program development involved defining activities, participants, and coordination needs; grant support involved translating research aims into staffing plans, budgets, and compliance considerations.
implementation: Fayana worked across faculty, staff, students, and community partners to coordinate activities and keep program development and grant preparation moving together.
methods: Community-engaged research practices, research administration, and program coordination.
deliverables: A professional development curriculum for underrepresented students, designed and implemented
Drafting, editing, compliance-review, and budget contributions to an NIH R01 grant application
risks: Grant preparation involves firm deadlines and compliance requirements; the program needed to serve students well while remaining feasible for the center.
results: Contributed to the timely, accurate, and compliant submission of a competitive NIH R01 funding proposal.
Designed and implemented a professional development curriculum that expanded access to research training and institutional support for underrepresented students.
resultsNote: The grant application's funding outcome is not published here pending verification.
lessons: This role connected research administration with program design, sharpening skills in staffing plans, budgets, and compliance that carry directly into research program management.

title: Public Health and Medical Anthropology Curriculum Development
summary: Designed and taught courses on race, health disparities, and applied medical anthropology, developed curricula and instructional materials, and supported curriculum review and program assessment.
context: As an Assistant Professor of Medical Anthropology at the University of Memphis from August 2019 to May 2021, Fayana combined teaching, curriculum development, program assessment, and student mentoring.
need: Students needed courses that connected anthropological research with applied public health concerns, taught through engaging methods and tied to measurable learning objectives. The program also needed faculty contributions to curriculum review, assessment, and administrative planning.
goals: Design and deliver courses on race, health disparities, and applied medical anthropology.
Connect course content to measurable learning objectives.
Support curriculum review, program assessment, and administrative planning.
Mentor students in research and community engagement.
stakeholders: Students, departmental faculty and administrators, and the communities connected to applied coursework.
scope: Course design and instruction, curriculum and instructional material development, program assessment support, and student mentoring.
responsibilities: Designed and taught six undergraduate and graduate courses related to race, health disparities, and applied medical anthropology.
Developed learning management system materials and interactive learning activities aligned with course objectives using instructional design principles.
Developed in-class surveys to assess comprehension and satisfaction, and revised course content based on student feedback.
Supported curriculum review and administrative planning through committee service.
Supervised six undergraduate and graduate student practicum placements.
Published peer-reviewed work on grandparent caregiving and presented at national and international conferences.
planning: Curriculum development began with learning objectives, then built instructional materials, activities, and assessments aligned to them.
implementation: Courses used interactive and discussion-based methods suited to demanding topics such as race and health disparities, and mentoring extended learning into research and community engagement.
methods: Curriculum design, learning assessment, interactive and discussion-based instruction, and program assessment.
deliverables: Six undergraduate and graduate courses, designed and taught
Learning management system materials and interactive learning activities
Contributions to curriculum review and program assessment
risks: Teaching on race and health disparities requires careful facilitation to keep discussions productive and inclusive.
results: Designed and taught six undergraduate and graduate courses.
Supervised six undergraduate and graduate student practicum placements, strengthening students' applied research and implementation skills.
Published peer-reviewed work on grandparent caregiving and the social and cultural impact of caregiving on aging.
Secured funding for a research project on caregiving and social isolation in Memphis, Tennessee, and Detroit, Michigan.
resultsNote: Course titles and teaching evaluation results are not published here pending verification.
lessons: Designing curricula around measurable objectives reinforced the same discipline Fayana applies to program design: define the goal first, then build the work plan to reach it.
confidentialityNote: Student identities and individual student outcomes are never published.

title: Federally Funded Research Project Coordination
summary: Coordinated activities for a federally funded research project, including expenditure monitoring, expense reporting, data management, and supervision of undergraduate researchers.
context: Early in her career, Fayana served as Project Coordinator for a federally funded research project at the University of Arizona from 2009 to 2010.
need: Federally funded research requires disciplined coordination: schedules, documentation, financial monitoring, data management, and supervision must all run reliably for the project to meet its obligations.
goals: Keep project activities coordinated and documented.
Monitor expenditures and provide accurate monthly expense reporting.
Support sound data management and undergraduate research supervision.
stakeholders: The project's research team, undergraduate researchers, and university administration.
scope: Day-to-day project coordination, financial monitoring and reporting, data management support, and supervision of undergraduate research activities.
responsibilities: Coordinated activities for a federally funded research project.
Supported biweekly budget reviews with the Principal Investigator and coordinated with the Business Office Manager.
Prepared monthly expense reports and monitored project expenditures.
Conducted qualitative and quantitative data transcription and analysis.
Supervised and collaborated with undergraduate research assistants on research design, analysis, and presentation development.
Presented research findings at national conferences.
planning: Coordination work centered on keeping schedules, documentation, and reporting cycles organized and predictable.
implementation: Fayana managed monthly reporting rhythms, tracked expenditures, supported data management, and supervised undergraduate researchers' day-to-day activities.
methods: Project documentation and reporting, expenditure monitoring, and qualitative and quantitative transcription and analysis using MAXQDA and SAS, with reference management in EndNote.
risks: Federal funding carries reporting and stewardship obligations that demand accuracy and consistency.
resultsNote: The project's total funding amount is not published here pending verification. Verified outcome information will be added after review of approved project records.
lessons: This early role built the financial monitoring, documentation, and coordination habits that underpin Fayana's later program management work.

title: Science Journalism and Research Translation
summary: Interviewed researchers, fact-checked scientific information, wrote articles for the Science website, and produced a podcast episode translating research for broad audiences.
context: Fayana completed an editorial internship with Science Magazine, working across written and audio formats to translate technical research for broader audiences. The dates of this role are being confirmed against approved records.
need: Science journalism requires accuracy, clarity, and speed: technical research must be verified, distilled, and communicated in ways general audiences can trust and understand.
goals: Translate technical research accurately for broad audiences.
Maintain rigorous fact-checking standards.
Produce engaging digital and audio science content.
stakeholders: Editors, researchers, and the magazine's readership.
scope: Editorial research, interviewing, fact-checking, digital writing, and podcast production.
responsibilities: Interviewed researchers and conducted background research.
Fact-checked scientific information.
Wrote articles for the Science website.
Produced a podcast episode.
Supported digital science communication.
planning: Each piece began with background research and interviews to establish an accurate foundation before writing.
implementation: Fayana developed stories through interviews and verification, then produced articles and audio content for digital publication.
methods: Interviewing, background research, fact-checking, science writing, and podcast production.
risks: Science communication carries a duty of accuracy; errors damage both the publication's and the researcher's credibility.
resultsNote: Specific article and podcast details are not published here pending verification. Verified outcome information will be added after review of approved project records.
lessons: Fact-checking and research translation remain central to how Fayana communicates evidence to executives, communities, and general audiences today.
